w: What's tested Sexual differentiation: why the female tract is the default pathway, and what happens to the Müllerian and Wolffian ducts The ovary's zones, and how the follicle and its oocyte develop, from primordial follicle to corpus luteum Steroid production in the follicle (two cells, two gonadotropins: he called it a very important slide), the three estrogens, and what estradiol and progesterone do The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis: GnRH, FSH, LH, inhibin, KNDy neurons, and the switch from negative to positive feedback The menstrual cycle: follicular phase, the LH surge and ovulation, luteal phase and menses, with the matching changes in the uterus and cervix (comparing the follicular and luteal phases is "high yield for exam") Menopause, and the reproductive disorders on the last slide Dr. Matthew Madison, PhD, of the Department of Medicine, gave this lecture on Tuesday, November 10; his title slide calls it Female Reproductive Endocrinology. These notes follow his recorded lecture and his slides. He told the class he would focus on the hormonal piece, the endocrinology, and that most of the hour is about the ovaries: the hormones they make and how the follicle develops, with the uterus as it changes through the menstrual cycle. He also pointed out that the female cells line up with the male lecture's (theca cells with Leydig cells, granulosa cells with Sertoli cells, with similar enzymes), so studying one system helps with the other. What he stressed: comparing and contrasting the follicular and luteal phases ("high yield for exam"); the slide of who responds to what, FSH on granulosa cells and LH on theca cells ("very important slide, I'd know this slide pretty well"); the two regulatory enzymes, cholesterol desmolase and aromatase ("remember these two steps"); the three estrogens; the granulosa and theca cells ("remember those cells"); and why FSH barely rises at midcycle (inhibin). What he said you don't need: the other enzymes of the steroid pathway, the names of the in-between follicle stages, and the slide on the whole-body actions of the steroid hormones ("I'm not gonna test you on this"). Where the female tract comes from: the default pathway The first objective is sexual differentiation, and the female answer is simple: it is the default pathway. Nothing has to switch it on. There is no Y chromosome driving anything, so no testes form, and two things follow from the missing testes, one for each pair of ducts. No anti-Müllerian hormone, or AMH, because there are no testes to make it. Without AMH, the Müllerian ducts form. No testosterone, so the Wolffian ducts regress. They need testosterone to differentiate, and without it they fade away. Keep the pairs straight, because they are easy to swap: lack of AMH explains the Müllerian ducts, and lack of testosterone explains the Wolffian ducts. In both cases it is the absence of a male hormone that does the work, not something the ovary secretes. In class he added the third missing male hormone: with no DHT (and no testosterone), the external genitalia form as female, also by default, and the Müllerian ducts go on to form the fallopian tubes and the uterus. "What you need to understand," he said, is that without testosterone, DHT and anti-Müllerian hormone, "the default pathway is female reproductive development." The ovary and the tract The ovaries sit in the peritoneal cavity, close to the opening of the fallopian tube, but no duct joins them to it. The fimbriae at the end of the tube beat, and that beating sweeps the released oocyte into the tube. Fertilization happens in the fallopian tube. The speaker notes add that estrogen is high just before ovulation and causes contraction that helps trap the oocyte in the tube. The ovary has zones. The medulla and hilum hold the blood and lymphatic vessels. The cortex holds the ovarian follicles, the functional units of the ovary. Almost everything in this lecture is about how those follicles grow, make hormones and release their oocytes. The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis The control system runs from the hypothalamus, through the anterior pituitary, to the ovary. The hypothalamus releases GnRH, which travels down the hypophyseal portal system to the anterior pituitary, the adenohypophysis, and binds receptors on its secretory cells. Those cells respond by making LH and FSH, which enter the bloodstream. FSH and LH act mainly on the ovaries, making them produce estrogen and inhibin, and they regulate both the ovarian cycle and the menstrual cycle. The ovarian hormones feed back. Estrogen inhibits GnRH production in the hypothalamus: negative feedback. The speaker notes stress that the hypothalamic and pituitary hormones (GnRH, FSH and LH) and the gonadal hormones (the steroids and inhibin) exist in a dynamic equilibrium: each side is constantly adjusting to the other. What controls GnRH itself? GnRH neurons respond to sex steroids, glucocorticoids, inflammation, stress, drugs, body metabolism and nutrition. But they do not respond to these directly. A separate set of neurons, the KNDy neurons, act as a bridge between the GnRH neurons and those environmental and internal signals, and they are mainly responsible for regulating GnRH release. The K stands for kisspeptin: the slide's diagram feeds circadian rhythms, metabolism (through leptin) and kisspeptin production into GnRH control. The discovery of KNDy neurons changed how GnRH release is understood. In class he described the KNDy neurons as innervating and synapsing onto the GnRH neurons. What they pass on can be the menstrual rhythm, the circadian rhythm or metabolism: leptin is a signal that the body is metabolically adequate to reproduce, so it promotes GnRH release. On the other side, the sex steroids' feedback, inflammation, stress, hypoglycemia, drugs and prolactin inhibit GnRH, and FSH and LH fall with it. Two kinds of feedback The female axis uses both negative and positive feedback, and which one is running depends on the hormone and on how much of it there is. Progesterone gives negative feedback only, on both the hypothalamus and the pituitary. Estrogen can give both. At ordinary levels it suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH. But as follicles grow and estradiol keeps rising, it progressively sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH, so that just before ovulation GnRH sets off a burst of LH. That amplification of the pituitary's response is positive feedback. Inhibin, from the follicle, suppresses FSH, preferentially: it is why FSH rises so little at midcycle while LH surges. Positive feedback is what makes the female cyclical. The male has no positive feedback mechanism, so the male axis is acyclical: steady negative feedback and no surge. If a question asks why the female system cycles and the male system doesn't, the answer is estradiol's positive feedback. In class he put it simply: progesterone is "always going to be negative feedback"; estrogen is negative "the majority of the time," and positive at one point, the middle of the cycle. Estradiol, ordinary levels Negative, on GnRH, LH and FSH Most of the follicular phase Estradiol above about 200 picograms per milliliter Positive: sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH, so LH surges Midcycle, just before ovulation Progesterone Negative only, on GnRH, LH and FSH Luteal phase Inhibin Suppresses FSH (not LH) Made by the growing follicle's granulosa cells; keeps FSH's midcycle peak small; gone in menopause Making estrogen: two cells, two gonadotropins No single cell in the follicle makes estradiol from start to finish. The work is split between two cells, each run by its own gonadotropin. Theca cells respond to LH. LH increases the activity of cholesterol desmolase, also called P450scc or the side-chain cleavage enzyme, which turns cholesterol into pregnenolone. It is the rate-limiting step of estrogen synthesis, and the theca cells make testosterone, the precursor of estrogen (and some progesterone along the way). Theca cells have no aromatase, so their testosterone moves over to the granulosa cells. Granulosa cells respond to FSH; they carry the FSH receptors. FSH makes them express and activate aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to estrogen, 17-beta estradiol. The same aromatase also converts adrenal androgens such as androstenedione. The cells of the male lecture map straight on: theca cells are like Leydig cells (LH, testosterone), and granulosa cells are like Sertoli cells (FSH, aromatase). Each half depends on the other. Block LH and the theca cells stop supplying testosterone, so aromatase has nothing to convert. Block FSH and testosterone is still made, but it is not turned into estradiol. He called this "a very important slide" and said to know it well, because it shows who responds to what, as the Sertoli and Leydig cells do in the male. Both receptors are G protein-coupled (Gs). Of the enzymes, he only wants these two: "I don't care that you know most of those enzymes unless we're talking about aromatase or cholesterol desmolase." Aromatase is in males too, also turned up by FSH, but it is far more active, at higher levels, in females. The L14 histology lecture says the same thing in more general words: theca interna cells answer to LH and make androgens, the precursors of estrogen. Testosterone is the androgen these slides name. There is one twist at midcycle: the granulosa cells start to express LH receptors at midcycle, partly in preparation for the luteal phase, when they become lutein cells that answer to LH. The lecture says that without this the dominant follicle could not keep producing estrogen. (The slide ties it to FSH diminishing as inhibin rises toward ovulation. In class Dr. Madison described FSH the same way as Dr. Herr's L14 graph: it still rises at midcycle, just far less than LH, because inhibin holds it back.) FSH and LH also build the follicle. FSH promotes the transformation of primordial follicular cells into granulosa cells and increases their estrogen synthesis. LH stimulates the formation of theca cells at the secondary follicle stage and increases their testosterone synthesis. Gonadotropin LH FSH Enzyme it raises Cholesterol desmolase (P450scc), the rate-limiting step Aromatase Product Testosterone, the precursor (and some progesterone); no aromatase 17-beta estradiol, converted from testosterone Male counterpart Leydig cells Sertoli cells Receptors appear LH receptors in the theca interna, once the theca forms FSH receptors at the primary follicle; LH receptors added at midcycle The three estrogens Three estrogens appear on the biosynthesis slide, and each belongs to a different stage of life. In class: in the reproductive years the main estrogen is 17-beta estradiol, in pregnancy estriol, and in menopause estrone. Progesterone, the other main female sex steroid, is made along the way, as an intermediate on the path to testosterone. 17-beta estradiol The main estrogen from the ovary Testosterone from theca cells, converted by aromatase in granulosa cells Estrone The estrogen of menopause DHEA from the adrenal gland's zona reticularis Estriol The estrogen of pregnancy 16-hydroxy DHEA sulfate made by the fetus, sent to the placenta, where estriol is made Estrone outlasts the follicles because its precursor comes from the adrenal gland, not the ovary; that is why it becomes the dominant estrogen after menopause. "Remember this," he said: the adrenal cortex's DHEA is where most postmenopausal estrogen comes from, and estrone is not nearly as potent as estradiol. How a follicle grows Dr. Madison's slide gives follicle development in three stages. Stage 1. The primary oocyte grows, and the granulosa cells proliferate and nurture it. The primordial follicle becomes a primary follicle, defined by one or more cuboidal granulosa cells arranged in a single layer around the oocyte. As this happens the granulosa cells start to express FSH receptors. No follicle progresses beyond this first stage until puberty, so a follicle can be locked here for 13 to 50 years. Stage 2. During each menstrual cycle, a few follicles enter this sequence. Fluid and hormones accumulate in a cavity called the antrum, and the theca and granulosa cells keep growing. This is the Graafian follicle. Stage 3. A single Graafian follicle becomes the dominant follicle. On day 14 of a 28-day cycle it ruptures and releases the oocyte into the nearby fallopian tube. The step in between, the secondary follicle, brings two major changes: the granulosa cells form multiple layers around the oocyte, and the follicle acquires a theca. The single cuboidal layer of the primary follicle becomes a stratified, many-layered epithelium. The surrounding stroma develops a blood supply and differentiates into the theca interna and the theca externa, and the theca interna develops LH receptors. Growth from a primary to a fully grown secondary follicle is an active autocrine and paracrine process, driven by growth factors made by the oocyte. With FSH receptors on the granulosa cells and LH receptors on the theca, the follicle can now respond to both gonadotropins. In class he walked the same path. A girl is born with all the primordial follicles she will have, follicular cells wrapped around an oocyte, and none moves on until puberty. At the primary stage the follicular cells differentiate into granulosa cells ("remember those cells, because those are going to be important"), which nourish the oocyte and start making sex steroids. In the secondary follicle the granulosa cells proliferate, from a cuboidal arrangement to a many-layered, pseudostratified columnar look, and theca cells appear on the outside, "the second important cell to remember." Then the antrum forms. Several follicles can progress at the same time, but one becomes the dominant Graafian follicle and releases the oocyte; the others regress and form scar tissue. The in-between stage is "sometimes called tertiary, sometimes called antral," and he said he doesn't care as much about the intermediate phases: "just know that one of them is going to become the dominant follicle." The antrum of the Graafian follicle is filled with follicular fluid, a plasma exudate conditioned by secretions from the oocyte and the granulosa cells. Just before ovulation, the Graafian follicle has a high expression of LH receptors, which is what lets the LH surge act on it. Watch the names. These slides call the many-layered follicle with a theca the secondary follicle, and the follicle with an antrum the Graafian follicle. The L14 histology lecture names the same stages differently: early primary for one cuboidal layer, late primary for several layers with a theca, secondary for the follicle with an antrum, and mature Graafian for the large follicle about to ovulate. The order of events is the same in both, so learn the sequence and not just the labels. In class Dr. Madison called the in-between follicle with an antrum tertiary or antral and kept Graafian for the dominant follicle about to ovulate, close to L14's names. Primordial The resting follicle; none moves on before puberty Can wait 13 to 50 years Primary A single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells around the oocyte Granulosa cells start expressing FSH receptors Secondary (the histology lecture's late primary) Multiple granulosa layers and a theca (interna and externa) Theca interna develops LH receptors; growth driven by oocyte growth factors Graafian, with an antrum (the histology lecture's secondary, then mature Graafian) A fluid-filled antrum; a few start each cycle, one becomes dominant High LH receptor expression before ovulation Corpus luteum The ruptured follicle's remains, mostly granulosa cells Secretes steroid hormones, mainly progesterone in the luteal phase The oocyte's two meiotic divisions The oocyte in a growing follicle is a primary oocyte, and it stays one through all of follicle growth. It does not become a secondary oocyte until ovulation, when the factors that inhibit meiosis are suppressed or removed as a result of the LH surge. The surge triggers resumption of meiosis, and the first meiotic division is complete by the time the oocyte is ovulated. The second meiotic division is completed in the fallopian tube. In class he named the block: the antrum's fluid holds plasma proteins, growth factors and factors that arrest the cell cycle, among them oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), which keeps the oocyte "in a locked state" until ovulation. The LH surge lowers OMI, so meiosis resumes. The L14 histology lecture adds the detail behind that: the ovulated secondary oocyte waits at metaphase of meiosis two and finishes the division only if a sperm fertilizes it, which happens in the tube. The corpus luteum After rupture, the remaining elements of the follicle become the corpus luteum. It is made mostly of granulosa cells, with some theca cells, and it synthesizes and secretes the steroid hormones needed for implantation and for maintaining a zygote. What happens next depends on fertilization. If fertilization occurs, the placenta takes over hormone production. If it does not, the corpus luteum regresses over 14 days into a scar, the corpus albicans. In class he called it a "hormonal warehouse": the granulosa and theca cells left behind luteinize, some of the enzymes that ran the follicular phase are turned off, and progesterone is made at much higher levels, with some estradiol still made. The menstrual cycle: three phases Ovarian hormone secretion is cyclic, and the lecture divides a typical 28-day cycle into three parts: the follicular phase (about 14 days), midcycle, and the luteal phase (about 14 days). The graph on the slides is captioned as showing the dramatic rise in LH around ovulation, and the notes say LH stays fairly steady through the cycle until it surges just before ovulation. Follicular, or proliferative 0 to 14 The growing follicle 17-beta estradiol Estradiol negative on GnRH, LH and FSH Midcycle About 14, which is 14 days before menses The dominant follicle Estradiol above 200 picograms per milliliter, then the LH surge Estradiol positive; FSH rises too, a much smaller peak held down by inhibin Luteal, or secretory 14 to 28 The corpus luteum Progesterone Progesterone negative on GnRH, LH and FSH Menses Day 28 without fertilization Corpus luteum regression Abrupt loss of estrogen and progesterone Lining and blood sloughed off The L14 histology lecture counts the same 28 days by the uterus instead: menstrual phase days 1 to 5, proliferative phase days 5 to 14, secretory phase days 15 to 28. Dr. Madison counts by the ovary, with the follicular phase from day 0 to day 14 and menses at day 28, the end of one cycle and the start of the next. Both lectures put ovulation at about day 14 and match proliferative with follicular and secretory with luteal. Follicular phase, days 0 to 14 The follicular phase is also called the proliferative phase. It precedes ovulation and is the time of follicle development. It is dominated by estrogen: 17-beta estradiol increases markedly, and it prepares the endometrial lining to accept a fertilized ovum. Growth of the endometrium. Lengthening of the endometrial arteries. The start of watery cervical mucus. Helping to propel sperm. He called comparing this phase with the luteal phase "high yield for exam." It is proliferative in two places: the granulosa cells of the growing follicle and the endometrial lining. The mucus is watery and stretchy (he called it elastic), and it helps propel sperm toward the egg: the follicular phase is working toward fertilization. The hormonal control is a negative feedback loop: GnRH stimulates the synthesis and secretion of FSH and LH, FSH and LH stimulate estradiol secretion from the follicular cells, and estradiol feeds back negatively on GnRH, LH and FSH. Midcycle: the LH surge and ovulation Midcycle comes 14 days before menses, and it is ovulation, the release of the mature ovum. Ovulation follows a burst of estradiol. The loop is the same as in the follicular phase, GnRH to FSH and LH to estradiol, until plasma estradiol reaches a critical level, greater than 200 picograms per milliliter. That prompts the positive feedback mechanism, which sets off the surge of LH, and the surge causes ovulation. FSH rises along with it, but far less. In class he asked why, and answered it: as the follicle develops, inhibin rises, and inhibin "is going to preferentially inhibit FSH," feeding back on the anterior pituitary, "so that's why we don't call it an LH-FSH surge, we call it an LH surge." That agrees with Dr. Herr's cycle graph in L14, where FSH makes a small peak beside the LH surge, and with the slide's "FSH is suppressed by production of inhibin." He described the switch to positive feedback as happening at the hypothalamus; the slides describe estradiol sensitizing the pituitary to GnRH. Either way, it is estradiol above about 200 pg/mL that flips the feedback and sets off the LH surge. Preovulatory Graafian follicles have a high expression of LH receptors, and the surge does two things to them: it triggers resumption of meiosis and follicular rupture. The egg is released from the dominant follicle typically 24 to 36 hours after the surge. In response to the surge, collagenases rise and weaken the follicular wall, and prostaglandins rise and increase blood flow, so the mature follicle becomes weak enough to rupture. In class he summed up the surge's effects on the follicle as three: proteases such as collagenase degrade the collagen in its wall, prostaglandins raise its blood flow, and oocyte maturation inhibitor falls, so the first meiotic division can finish. The slides only draw the typical 28-day cycle, but they put midcycle at 14 days before menses and give the corpus luteum about 14 days. So in a cycle of a different length, the day of ovulation moves while the luteal half stays about the same: day 14 in a 28-day cycle, about day 18 in a 32-day cycle. Luteal phase, days 14 to 28 The luteal phase is also called the secretory phase. It follows ovulation and is driven by the corpus luteum. It is dominated by progesterone, which increases markedly and prepares the endometrium to receive the fertilized ovum. Proliferation of the endometrium slows. Endometrial secretions increase. Endometrial vasculature increases. Watery cervical mucus decreases, and the mucus becomes thick. This phase is working toward implantation, where the follicular phase worked toward fertilization. In class he added that the endometrial vasculature thickens and glycogen vacuoles form, so an embryo that implants has blood supply and an energy store, and that the thick mucus suits implantation rather than sperm. One more sign: progesterone acts on the hypothalamus to raise body temperature, so a slight rise in temperature, a "slight fever," is a feature of the luteal phase. The control loop now runs through progesterone: GnRH stimulates FSH and LH, they stimulate progesterone secretion, and progesterone feeds back negatively on GnRH, LH and FSH. Menses On day 28, without fertilization, the endometrial lining and blood are sloughed off. Menses is prompted by the regression of the corpus luteum and the abrupt loss of estrogen and progesterone that follows. In class: the corpus luteum makes hormones for about 14 days, give or take, then becomes the corpus albicans, and losing its steroids is the signal for the endometrial lining to be shed. Estrogen and progesterone on the uterus The uterus has two layers, and the two hormones act on each of them. Endometrium Growth; endometrial arteries lengthen Enhances and sustains growth; slows proliferation; more secretions and vasculature Myometrium Contraction Relaxation Cervical mucus Watery; helps propel sperm Thick Feedback Negative, or positive above about 200 picograms per milliliter Negative only In class he described the two layers by their jobs: the endometrium is where implantation and the embryo's first development happen, and the myometrium is the muscular layer that matters for carrying and delivering a baby. Counted by the uterus, the cycle is menstrual (the lining sloughs), proliferative (the functional layer grows) and secretory (the vessels widen and glycogen vacuoles form, ready for implantation). The uterine cycle is an overlay of the ovarian cycle on the endometrial cycle: estrogen grows the endometrium during the follicular phase, and progesterone enhances that growth and its blood supply during the luteal phase. The growth is timed to ovulation and to the oocyte's transport toward fertilization, so the lining is ready for implantation. His next slide, the whole-body actions of estrogen and progesterone (the skin, memory, the mammary glands, GI motility, the brain and the heart), is one he said he won't test: "I'm not gonna test you on this." Menopause Menopause is the cessation of the menstrual cycle. It comes with complete atresia of all the remaining follicles; atresia is a form of programmed cell death, and the number of functioning follicles falls in the years before. Then the chain of feedback runs backward. Estradiol secretion declines, because granulosa cells no longer make estradiol or inhibin. With nothing left to give negative feedback, GnRH, LH and FSH all rise. The speaker notes say GnRH goes sky high, and rising GnRH can lead to hot flashes. In class he said hot flashes have been linked to that GnRH peak, though research linking the symptoms to the hormone levels is still going on. Estrone becomes the dominant estrogen, made from adrenal DHEA, and not nearly as potent as estradiol. The symptoms on the slide: thinning of the vaginal epithelium, decreased vaginal secretions, decreased breast mass, accelerated bone loss, and vascular instability, the hot flashes. In class he singled out the vaginal epithelium: estradiol is especially important for its growth and maintenance, and losing it affects every female reproductive structure. Reproductive disorders The last content slide groups reproductive disorders, attributed to hormonal disorders, into three kinds. Disorders of sexual differentiation, with Turner syndrome as the slide's example. Primary amenorrhea: periods never start. The slide names primary and secondary amenorrhea without defining them; these are the standard definitions. Secondary amenorrhea: periods that had started stop. The causes listed are pregnancy, lactation, menopause and hyperprolactinemia, an increase in prolactin. In class he described primary amenorrhea as usually genetic, with Turner syndrome as his example: one X chromosome is partly or completely lost, the ovaries are fully or partly malformed, the follicles can't go through their staged, cyclic development, and the person can't reproduce. So Turner syndrome sits under disorders of sexual differentiation on the slide and under primary amenorrhea in class; both are right. He then explained each cause of secondary amenorrhea: in menopause estradiol is lost; in pregnancy LH and FSH lose their normal cycle; in lactation, and with a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor, prolactin is high, and prolactin turns GnRH down, so FSH, LH and the sex steroids fall and the cycle stops. Amenorrhea is the absence of menstruation, often defined as missing one or more menstrual periods. Reading a hormone pattern Most applied questions on this lecture hand you a pattern and ask where in the cycle, or in life, the patient is. Work from the feedback rules above. Estradiol rising, FSH and LH held down Follicular phase: negative feedback Estradiol above 200 picograms per milliliter, LH rising steeply, progesterone low Midcycle, just before ovulation: positive feedback Progesterone high, FSH and LH low Luteal phase: a working corpus luteum Estrogen and progesterone falling abruptly End of the luteal phase: menses is next Estradiol low; FSH, LH and GnRH high Menopause: no follicles, no negative feedback Low progesterone in the luteal phase and no LH surge No ovulation, so no corpus luteum formed
